subject: chemistry

items.q: What is the oxidation state of nitrogen in the ammonium ion, NH₄⁺?
items.why:
Students first meet oxidation states on monatomic ions, where the oxidation state really is the ionic charge (Fe³⁺ is +3). The rule is carried over to polyatomic ions, where the charge belongs to the whole ion. The charge of a polyatomic ion is the SUM of the oxidation states of all its atoms. Assign the known states (H +1, O −2) first, then find the unknown state that makes the sum equal the ion's charge.

Working: Let the oxidation state of N be x. H is +1. Sum = charge on ion: x + 4(+1) = +1, so x = −3.
items.specStatementText: Oxidation and reduction can be described in terms of electron transfer, change in oxidation state, oxygen gain/loss or hydrogen loss/gain.
items.working: Let the oxidation state of N be x. H is +1. Sum = charge on ion: x + 4(+1) = +1, so x = −3.

items.q:
Chlorine reacts with aqueous iron(II) ions:
2Fe²⁺(aq) + Cl₂(aq) → 2Fe³⁺(aq) + 2Cl⁻(aq)
Which species is the oxidizing agent in this reaction?
items.correct: Cl₂, since it gains electrons and so is itself reduced
items.misconception: Fe²⁺, since it loses electrons and so is itself oxidized
items.why: Widely reported in chemistry-education research: the grammar of 'oxidizing agent' suggests the agent undergoes oxidation, in the same way that a 'cleaning agent' might be thought to become clean. An agent does something to another species. An oxidizing agent takes electrons from another species, oxidizing it, and is therefore reduced. The reducing agent gives electrons and is oxidized.
items.specStatementText: Oxidation and reduction can be described in terms of electron transfer, change in oxidation state, oxygen gain/loss or hydrogen loss/gain.
items.random_wrong: Cl⁻, since it is the species holding the gained electrons

items.q: Which compound is correctly named?
items.correct: K₂Cr₂O₇, potassium dichromate(VI)
items.misconception: K₂MnO₄, potassium manganate(IV)
items.why: Numerical prefixes (di-, tri-) do count atoms in names such as carbon dioxide, and in several common compounds (FeCl₃, iron(III) chloride) the numeral happens to equal a subscript, which reinforces the idea. The numeral always gives the oxidation state of the element immediately before it. Work it out from the formula: in MnO₂, x + 2(−2) = 0, so x = +4.
items.specStatementText: Oxidation and reduction can be described in terms of electron transfer, change in oxidation state, oxygen gain/loss or hydrogen loss/gain.
items.random_wrong: Fe₂(SO₄)₃, iron(VI) sulfate

items.q: Which half-equation correctly shows the conversion of MnO₄⁻(aq) into Mn²⁺(aq) in acidic solution?
items.correct: MnO₄⁻ + 8H⁺ + 5e⁻ → Mn²⁺ + 4H₂O
items.misconception: MnO₄⁻ + 8H⁺ + 2e⁻ → Mn²⁺ + 4H₂O
items.why:
Students learn simple metal half-equations first (Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu, Zn → Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻), in which the electron count does equal the ionic charge, and apply the pattern to all half-equations. The electron count equals the change in oxidation state (per atom × number of atoms), and it must make the total charge on each side equal. Check the charge balance after writing the half-equation.

Working: O: 4 O on the left → 4H₂O on the right. H: 8 H in 4H₂O → 8H⁺ on the left. Charge: left −1 + 8 = +7, right +2, so add 5e⁻ to the left. Check: Mn +7 → +2 is a gain of 5 electrons.
items.specStatementText: Half-equations separate the processes of oxidation and reduction, showing the loss or gain of electrons.
items.random_wrong: MnO₄⁻ + 8H⁺ → Mn²⁺ + 4H₂O + 5e⁻
items.working: O: 4 O on the left → 4H₂O on the right. H: 8 H in 4H₂O → 8H⁺ on the left. Charge: left −1 + 8 = +7, right +2, so add 5e⁻ to the left. Check: Mn +7 → +2 is a gain of 5 electrons.

items.q: In acidic solution, MnO₄⁻(aq) is reduced to Mn²⁺(aq) and Fe²⁺(aq) is oxidized to Fe³⁺(aq). In the balanced overall redox equation, what amount of Fe²⁺ reacts with 1 mol of MnO₄⁻?
items.correct: 5 mol
items.misconception: 1 mol
items.why:
Adding equations looks like simple algebra, and in many first examples (Zn/Cu²⁺) the electron numbers already match, so the multiplying step is never practised. An overall equation contains no free electrons. Multiply so the electrons match (MnO₄⁻ gains 5e⁻, Fe²⁺ loses 1e⁻, so 5Fe²⁺ per MnO₄⁻), then add.

Working: Mn: +7 → +2, a gain of 5e⁻ per MnO₄⁻ (MnO₄⁻ + 8H⁺ + 5e⁻ → Mn²⁺ + 4H₂O). Fe: +2 → +3, a loss of 1e⁻ per Fe²⁺ (Fe²⁺ → Fe³⁺ + e⁻). Electrons lost = electrons gained, so the iron half-equation is multiplied by 5: 5 mol Fe²⁺ react with 1 mol MnO₄⁻.
items.specStatementText: Half-equations separate the processes of oxidation and reduction, showing the loss or gain of electrons.
items.random_wrong: 2 mol
items.working: Mn: +7 → +2, a gain of 5e⁻ per MnO₄⁻ (MnO₄⁻ + 8H⁺ + 5e⁻ → Mn²⁺ + 4H₂O). Fe: +2 → +3, a loss of 1e⁻ per Fe²⁺ (Fe²⁺ → Fe³⁺ + e⁻). Electrons lost = electrons gained, so the iron half-equation is multiplied by 5: 5 mol Fe²⁺ react with 1 mol MnO₄⁻.

items.q: Using positions in the periodic table, which of these metals would be expected to be oxidized most readily?
items.correct: rubidium
items.misconception: lithium
items.why: The alkali-metal and halogen trends are often taught in the same lesson and remembered as a single rule ('reactivity increases down/up the group') without the reason, which depends on whether electrons are lost or gained. Both trends follow from distance of the outer shell from the nucleus. Larger atoms lose electrons more easily (metals more reactive down the group) but attract an added electron less strongly (halogens less reactive down the group).
items.specStatementText: The relative ease of oxidation and reduction of an element in a group can be predicted from its position in the periodic table. The reactions between metals and aqueous metal ions demonstrate the relative ease of oxidation of different metals.
items.random_wrong: aluminium

items.q: Which statement about the relative ease of reduction of the halogens is correct?
items.correct: Chlorine is reduced more readily than bromine, as its atoms are smaller.
items.misconception: Bromine is reduced more readily than chlorine, as its nucleus has more protons.
items.why: Nuclear charge is taught as the cause of attraction, and 'more protons, more attraction' is applied without taking distance and shielding into account. Attraction for outer electrons depends on nuclear charge, distance and shielding together. Down a group the increase in distance and shielding outweighs the increase in protons.
items.specStatementText: The relative ease of oxidation and reduction of an element in a group can be predicted from its position in the periodic table. The reactions between metals and aqueous metal ions demonstrate the relative ease of oxidation of different metals.
items.random_wrong: Iodine is reduced more readily than bromine, as it is further down group 17.

items.q:
A student places three metals, X, Y and Z, in solutions of each other's nitrates. X forms a coating in solutions of Y²⁺ and of Z²⁺; Y forms a coating in the solution of Z²⁺ only; Z shows no change in either solution.
Which of these is the strongest oxidizing agent?
items.correct: the ion Z²⁺
items.misconception: the ion X²⁺
items.why: 'Reactive' is treated as a property of the element in all its forms, so the reactivity of the metal is transferred to its ion. A metal that loses electrons easily forms an ion that has little tendency to regain them. The metal and its ion are at opposite ends of the same half-equation, so a strong reducing agent (the metal) has a weak oxidizing agent as its ion.
items.specStatementText: The relative ease of oxidation and reduction of an element in a group can be predicted from its position in the periodic table. The reactions between metals and aqueous metal ions demonstrate the relative ease of oxidation of different metals.
items.random_wrong: the metal X

items.q: Which equation correctly represents the reaction of aluminium with dilute hydrochloric acid?
items.correct: 2Al(s) + 6HCl(aq) → 2AlCl₃(aq) + 3H₂(g)
items.misconception: Al(s) + 3HCl(aq) → AlCl₃(aq) + H₂(g)
items.why: The magnesium and zinc reactions are the standard classroom examples, and their 1 : 1 metal : H₂ ratio is copied instead of balancing electrons or charges for each metal. Work from the ion charges: each metal atom loses as many electrons as its ionic charge, and every two electrons reduce 2H⁺ to one H₂. Aluminium (3+) therefore gives 3 H₂ per 2 Al.
items.specStatementText: Acids react with reactive metals to release hydrogen.
items.random_wrong: 2Al(s) + 6HCl(aq) → 2AlCl₃(aq) + 6H(g)

items.q: Aluminium reacts with excess dilute sulfuric acid. What amount of hydrogen gas is produced when 0.10 mol of aluminium reacts completely?
items.correct: 0.15 mol
items.misconception: 0.30 mol
items.why:
Students count the H atoms gained or lost and forget that hydrogen is supplied or released as diatomic H₂. Hydrogen is diatomic. Count the H atoms gained and divide by two, or count one H₂ per π bond.

Working: Al → Al³⁺ + 3e⁻ and 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂, so 2Al(s) + 3H₂SO₄(aq) → Al₂(SO₄)₃(aq) + 3H₂(g). n(H₂) = 0.10 mol × 3/2 = 0.15 mol.
items.specStatementText: Acids react with reactive metals to release hydrogen.
items.random_wrong: 0.10 mol
items.working: Al → Al³⁺ + 3e⁻ and 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂, so 2Al(s) + 3H₂SO₄(aq) → Al₂(SO₄)₃(aq) + 3H₂(g). n(H₂) = 0.10 mol × 3/2 = 0.15 mol.

items.q:
A voltaic cell is made from a Zn(s)|Zn²⁺(aq) half-cell and a Cu(s)|Cu²⁺(aq) half-cell. Zinc is oxidized more readily than copper.
Which statement about the zinc electrode is correct?
items.correct: It is negative, as zinc is oxidized there and releases electrons.
items.misconception: It is positive, as oxidation takes place at a positive anode.
items.why: Electrolysis is usually taught before voltaic cells, and the rule 'anions go to the positive anode' is learned as a definition of the anode. Name electrodes by the reaction: oxidation at the anode, reduction at the cathode. In a voltaic cell the anode releases electrons into the wire, so it is negative.
items.specStatementText: Oxidation occurs at the anode and reduction occurs at the cathode in electrochemical cells.
items.random_wrong: It is the cathode, as positive zinc ions are formed there.

items.q: Molten sodium chloride is electrolysed. Which statement about the electrode connected to the positive terminal of the DC supply is correct?
items.correct: It is the anode, where chloride ions lose electrons.
items.misconception: It is the cathode, as the cathode is the positive electrode.
items.why: Widely reported in chemistry-education research on electrochemistry: after studying voltaic cells, students fix 'anode = negative' as a definition and carry it into electrolytic cells. The anode is defined by oxidation. In an electrolytic cell the supply pulls electrons out of the anode, so it is positive; anions are oxidized there.
items.specStatementText: Oxidation occurs at the anode and reduction occurs at the cathode in electrochemical cells.
items.random_wrong: It is the cathode, where chloride ions become oxidized.

items.q:
A voltaic cell is made from Zn(s)|Zn²⁺(aq) and Cu(s)|Cu²⁺(aq) half-cells joined by a salt bridge containing KNO₃(aq). Zinc is the anode.
Which describes how charge moves through the salt bridge?
items.correct: K⁺ ions move to the copper half-cell and NO₃⁻ ions to the zinc half-cell.
items.misconception: Electrons move through it from the zinc half-cell to the copper half-cell.
items.why: Widely reported in chemistry-education research: students picture an electric circuit as a single loop of electrons, so the solution part of the circuit must carry electrons too. Free electrons do not travel through aqueous solutions. The circuit is completed in solution by ions: cations and anions move in opposite directions, keeping each solution neutral.
items.specStatementText: A primary (voltaic) cell is an electrochemical cell that converts energy from spontaneous redox reactions to electrical energy.
items.random_wrong: NO₃⁻ ions move to the copper half-cell, attracted by its positive electrode.

items.q:
A voltaic cell is made from a Mg(s)|Mg²⁺(aq) half-cell and an Ag(s)|Ag⁺(aq) half-cell. Magnesium is oxidized far more readily than silver.
Which describes the flow of electrons in this cell?
items.correct: From Mg to Ag through the wire, released as Mg atoms are oxidized
items.misconception: From Ag to Mg through the wire, since current leaves the positive terminal
items.why: Circuit diagrams in physics show conventional current from + to −, and students take this to be the direction of electron movement. Conventional current (+ to −) was defined before the electron was discovered. Electrons carry negative charge and move from − to +, i.e. from anode to cathode in a voltaic cell.
items.specStatementText: A primary (voltaic) cell is an electrochemical cell that converts energy from spontaneous redox reactions to electrical energy.
items.random_wrong: From Mg to Ag through the wire, returning to Mg through the salt bridge

items.q:
During discharge of a lead–acid cell, the reaction at the negative electrode is:
Pb(s) + SO₄²⁻(aq) → PbSO₄(s) + 2e⁻
Which half-equation shows the reaction at this electrode while the cell is being charged?
items.correct: PbSO₄(s) + 2e⁻ → Pb(s) + SO₄²⁻(aq)
items.misconception: Pb(s) + SO₄²⁻(aq) → PbSO₄(s) + 2e⁻
items.why: 'Charging' is pictured as filling the cell with energy or electricity, with no idea that the chemical change must be undone. Discharge converts reactants to products. Charging must convert those products back into the reactants, so each half-equation is reversed and the electrode that was the anode becomes the cathode.
items.specStatementText: Secondary (rechargeable) cells involve redox reactions that can be reversed using electrical energy.
items.random_wrong: PbSO₄(s) → Pb(s) + SO₄²⁻(aq) + 2e⁻

items.q: Which statement about fuel cells, primary cells and secondary cells is correct?
items.correct: A fuel cell supplies electricity for as long as its fuel and oxygen are supplied.
items.misconception: A secondary cell stores electricity, which it releases unchanged on discharge.
items.why: Everyday language ('the battery is full of charge', 'storing power') describes cells as containers of electricity. A cell stores energy chemically. As it discharges, electrons are transferred in a redox reaction; the reactants are used up and products form. Charging uses electrical energy to regenerate the reactants.
items.specStatementText: Secondary (rechargeable) cells involve redox reactions that can be reversed using electrical energy.
items.random_wrong: A hydrogen fuel cell produces only water, so using one causes no pollution of any kind.

items.q: Molten lead(II) bromide is electrolysed using graphite electrodes. How is the electric current conducted through the molten lead(II) bromide itself?
items.correct: By Pb²⁺ and Br⁻ ions, already present, moving to the electrodes
items.misconception: By delocalized electrons released when the solid melts
items.why: Electrical conduction is first met in metals and explained by delocalized electrons, so every conductor is assumed to conduct in the same way. There are two kinds of conductor: metals (delocalized electrons) and electrolytes (mobile ions). In an electrolytic cell electrons carry the current in the wires and ions carry it in the electrolyte.
items.specStatementText: An electrolytic cell is an electrochemical cell that converts electrical energy to chemical energy by bringing about non-spontaneous reactions.
items.random_wrong: By electrons moving through the melt from the cathode to the anode

items.q: Molten potassium iodide, KI(l), is electrolysed with inert electrodes. Which half-equation shows the reaction at the anode?
items.correct: 2I⁻ → I₂ + 2e⁻
items.why: The phrase 'loses its charge' is used informally for discharging at an electrode, and students translate losing a charge into losing electrons. A positive ion is short of electrons. To become neutral it must gain electrons equal to its charge; the ion is reduced. Losing electrons would make the charge more positive.
items.specStatementText: An electrolytic cell is an electrochemical cell that converts electrical energy to chemical energy by bringing about non-spontaneous reactions.

items.q: Propan-1-ol is converted into propanoic acid by heating it under reflux with an acidified oxidizing agent. Why is reflux used?
items.correct: Reflux returns condensed vapour, so propanal stays in the flask to be oxidized.
items.misconception: Reflux removes propanal from the flask as soon as it has formed.
items.why: Both methods use a condenser and heating, and the difference (vertical condenser returning liquid versus a condenser leading to a collecting vessel) is remembered as a picture rather than by its purpose. Reflux = vapour returns to the flask, so the reaction goes to completion (carboxylic acid). Distillation = vapour is collected elsewhere, so the aldehyde escapes further oxidation.
items.specStatementText: Functional groups in organic compounds may undergo oxidation.
items.random_wrong: Reflux converts propan-1-ol straight to the acid, with no propanal formed.

items.q: 2-methylpropan-2-ol, (CH₃)₃COH, is heated with an acidified oxidizing agent under the conditions that oxidize ethanol. Which statement is correct?
items.correct: It is not oxidized, as its C–OH carbon carries no hydrogen atom.
items.misconception: It is oxidized to a ketone, as its OH group is on a central carbon.
items.why: Students learn 'end of chain → aldehyde, middle of chain → ketone' as a positional rule, and tertiary alcohols (OH on a central carbon) are fitted into the 'middle' category. Use the classification, not the position: count the carbons bonded to the C–OH carbon. Tertiary (three) means no H on that carbon, so no oxidation.
items.specStatementText: Functional groups in organic compounds may undergo oxidation.
items.random_wrong: It is oxidized to a carboxylic acid if it is heated for long enough.

items.q: Propan-1-ol is heated under reflux with an excess of acidified oxidizing agent, represented by [O]. Which equation represents the overall change?
items.correct: CH₃CH₂CH₂OH + 2[O] → CH₃CH₂COOH + H₂O
items.misconception: CH₃CH₂CH₂OH + [O] → CH₃COCH₃ + H₂O
items.why: Both contain a C=O group and are learned together as 'carbonyl compounds'; the difference in the position of the C=O is not used when predicting products. Oxidation and reduction do not move the functional group along the chain. An end-of-chain carbon (primary alcohol, aldehyde, carboxylic acid) stays at the end; a C–OH or C=O within the chain (secondary alcohol, ketone) stays within the chain.
items.specStatementText: Functional groups in organic compounds may undergo oxidation.
items.random_wrong: CH₃CH₂CH₂OH + [O] → CH₃CH₂CHO + H₂O

items.q: Butanone, CH₃COCH₂CH₃, is reduced. What is the organic product?
items.correct: CH₃CH(OH)CH₂CH₃
items.misconception: CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂OH
items.why: Most worked examples of reduction start from carboxylic acids or aldehydes, so 'reduction gives a primary alcohol' is generalized. Reduction adds H to the C=O carbon and to the O. The OH stays on the same carbon as the original C=O, so a ketone's middle carbon gives a secondary alcohol.
items.specStatementText: Functional groups in organic compounds may undergo reduction.
items.random_wrong: CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₃

items.q: Carbonyl compounds are reduced by reducing agents that act as a source of hydride ions, H⁻. What is the role of the hydride ion?
items.correct: It adds hydrogen to the carbon of the C=O group, so the compound is reduced.
items.misconception: It removes hydrogen from the carbonyl compound, which reduces the compound.
items.why: Students learn 'gain of oxygen = oxidation' first and generalize 'gaining something = oxidation', so the hydrogen definitions are recalled the wrong way round. Hydrogen is less electronegative than carbon, oxygen more. Gaining oxygen lowers the electron density on carbon (oxidation); gaining hydrogen raises it (reduction). So oxidation is gain of O or loss of H; reduction is loss of O or gain of H.
items.specStatementText: Functional groups in organic compounds may undergo reduction.
items.random_wrong: It acts as an acid, donating a proton, H⁺, to the oxygen of the C=O group.

items.q: Which describes the reduction of propanoic acid, CH₃CH₂COOH?
items.correct: Propanal forms first and is then reduced to propan-1-ol.
items.misconception: Propan-1-ol forms in a single step, with no aldehyde formed.
items.why: Summary equations such as CH₃CH₂OH + 2[O] → CH₃COOH + H₂O hide the intermediate, and the aldehyde is seen only when it is deliberately isolated. The carbon bearing the functional group changes one oxidation level at a time: alcohol → aldehyde → carboxylic acid. The aldehyde can be isolated by distillation, which shows it is a genuine intermediate.
items.specStatementText: Functional groups in organic compounds may undergo reduction.
items.random_wrong: Propanone forms first and is then reduced to propan-2-ol.

items.q: Hex-1-en-5-yne, CH₂=CHCH₂CH₂C≡CH, reacts completely with excess hydrogen in the presence of a nickel catalyst. What amount of H₂ reacts with 1 mol of hex-1-en-5-yne?
items.correct: 3 mol
items.misconception: 2 mol
items.why:
Hydrogenation is taught mainly with alkenes (one H₂ per C=C), and the rule 'one H₂ per multiple bond' is not revised for alkynes. Count the π bonds: a double bond has one, a triple bond two. Each H₂ removes one π bond.

Working: π bonds: C=C has 1, C≡C has 2, total 3. One H₂ per π bond: 3 mol H₂ per mol. Check: C₆H₈ + 3H₂ → C₆H₁₄.
items.specStatementText: Reduction of unsaturated compounds by the addition of hydrogen lowers the degree of unsaturation.
items.random_wrong: 5 mol
items.working: π bonds: C=C has 1, C≡C has 2, total 3. One H₂ per π bond: 3 mol H₂ per mol. Check: C₆H₈ + 3H₂ → C₆H₁₄.

items.q: Why is the standard electrode potential of the hydrogen half-cell, H⁺(aq) + e⁻ ⇌ ½H₂(g), given as 0 V?
items.correct: It is assigned by convention as the reference for other half-cells.
items.misconception: No oxidation or reduction occurs at the hydrogen electrode.
items.why: Zero is associated with 'nothing happening', and the platinum electrode is described as inert. Zero is simply the chosen reference point, like sea level for altitude. Connected to other half-cells, the hydrogen electrode acts as an anode or a cathode.
items.specStatementText: The hydrogen half-cell H⁺(aq) + e⁻ ⇌ ½H₂(g) is assigned a standard electrode potential of zero by convention. It is used in the measurement of standard electrode potential, E⦵.
items.random_wrong: Its absolute potential has been measured directly and found to be zero.

items.q:
Standard electrode potentials:
Mg²⁺(aq) + 2e⁻ ⇌ Mg(s)   E⦵ = −2.37 V
Zn²⁺(aq) + 2e⁻ ⇌ Zn(s)   E⦵ = −0.76 V
Cu²⁺(aq) + 2e⁻ ⇌ Cu(s)   E⦵ = +0.34 V
Ag⁺(aq) + e⁻ ⇌ Ag(s)   E⦵ = +0.80 V
Which species is the strongest oxidizing agent?
items.correct: Ag⁺(aq), as its E⦵ value is the most positive
items.misconception: Mg²⁺(aq), as its E⦵ value is the largest in size
items.why: Students compare magnitudes as they would for many other quantities and treat the minus sign as a direction marker to be ignored. E⦵ values are on a scale running from very negative (the reduced form readily oxidized) to very positive (the oxidized form readily reduced). Compare signed values.
items.specStatementText: The hydrogen half-cell H⁺(aq) + e⁻ ⇌ ½H₂(g) is assigned a standard electrode potential of zero by convention. It is used in the measurement of standard electrode potential, E⦵.
items.random_wrong: Mg(s), as it is the species most readily oxidized

items.q:
Standard electrode potentials:
Fe³⁺(aq) + e⁻ ⇌ Fe²⁺(aq)   E⦵ = +0.77 V
Cu²⁺(aq) + 2e⁻ ⇌ Cu(s)   E⦵ = +0.34 V
Which statement about the reaction Cu(s) + 2Fe³⁺(aq) → Cu²⁺(aq) + 2Fe²⁺(aq) is correct?
items.correct: It is spontaneous as written, since E⦵cell = +0.43 V
items.misconception: It is spontaneous as written, since E⦵cell = +1.20 V
items.why:
Students have learned to scale enthalpy changes with the equation in Hess's law and apply the same rule to electrode potentials. Doubling the equation doubles the charge transferred and the energy, but not the energy per coulomb, which is what E⦵ measures. The amount scaling is carried by n in ΔG⦵ = −nFE⦵cell.

Working: Cathode (reduction): Fe³⁺ + e⁻ → Fe²⁺, E⦵ = +0.77 V. Anode (oxidation): Cu → Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻, E⦵ = +0.34 V. E⦵cell = +0.77 − (+0.34) = +0.43 V > 0, so the reaction is spontaneous as written.
items.specStatementText: Standard cell potential, E⦵cell, can be calculated from standard electrode potentials. E⦵cell has a positive value for a spontaneous reaction.
items.random_wrong: It is spontaneous in reverse, since E⦵cell = −0.43 V
items.working: Cathode (reduction): Fe³⁺ + e⁻ → Fe²⁺, E⦵ = +0.77 V. Anode (oxidation): Cu → Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻, E⦵ = +0.34 V. E⦵cell = +0.77 − (+0.34) = +0.43 V > 0, so the reaction is spontaneous as written.

items.q:
For the cell reaction Mg(s) + 2Ag⁺(aq) → Mg²⁺(aq) + 2Ag(s):
E⦵(Mg²⁺/Mg) = −2.37 V; E⦵(Ag⁺/Ag) = +0.80 V; F = 96 500 C mol⁻¹
What is ΔG⦵ for the reaction as written?
items.correct: −612 kJ mol⁻¹
items.misconception: −306 kJ mol⁻¹
items.why:
Students remember the product 'F × E' and drop n, particularly when the electrons do not appear in the overall equation. Find n from the half-equations: the number of electrons that cancel when the half-equations are combined. Multiply by it.

Working: E⦵cell = E⦵(cathode) − E⦵(anode) = +0.80 − (−2.37) = +3.17 V. n = 2. ΔG⦵ = −nFE⦵cell = −2 × 96 500 C mol⁻¹ × 3.17 V = −611 810 J mol⁻¹ = −612 kJ mol⁻¹ (3 s.f.).
items.specStatementText: The equation ΔG⦵ = −nFE⦵cell shows the relationship between standard change in Gibbs energy and standard cell potential for a reaction.
items.random_wrong: −766 kJ mol⁻¹
items.working: E⦵cell = E⦵(cathode) − E⦵(anode) = +0.80 − (−2.37) = +3.17 V. n = 2. ΔG⦵ = −nFE⦵cell = −2 × 96 500 C mol⁻¹ × 3.17 V = −611 810 J mol⁻¹ = −612 kJ mol⁻¹ (3 s.f.).

items.q:
Concentrated NaCl(aq) is electrolysed with inert electrodes.
Cl₂(g) + 2e⁻ ⇌ 2Cl⁻(aq)   E⦵ = +1.36 V
O₂(g) + 4H⁺(aq) + 4e⁻ ⇌ 2H₂O(l)   E⦵ = +1.23 V
What is the main product at the anode, and why?
items.correct: Chlorine, as the high Cl⁻ concentration favours oxidation of Cl⁻ over water
items.misconception: Oxygen, as E⦵ values decide the product whatever the Cl⁻ concentration
items.why: E⦵ comparison is taught as the method for predicting products, and the standard-conditions restriction (1 mol dm⁻³) is overlooked. E⦵ values refer to standard (1 mol dm⁻³) conditions and do not by themselves decide the product. Experimentally, concentrated NaCl(aq) gives mainly chlorine at the anode and dilute NaCl(aq) mainly oxygen, so the concentration of Cl⁻ must be taken into account.
items.specStatementText: During electrolysis of aqueous solutions, competing reactions can occur at the anode and cathode, including the oxidation and reduction of water.
items.random_wrong: Hydrogen, as H⁺ ions from the water are attracted to the anode

items.q: CuSO₄(aq) is electrolysed first with graphite electrodes and then with copper electrodes. Which statement explains the difference at the anode?
items.correct: With copper electrodes, the anode itself is oxidized to Cu²⁺, so no oxygen forms.
items.misconception: There is no difference: water is oxidized to oxygen at both types of anode.
items.why: Most electrolysis examples use inert electrodes, so electrodes are thought of as passive connectors. An anode made of a metal that is more easily oxidized than water takes part: Cu(s) → Cu²⁺(aq) + 2e⁻ (E⦵ +0.34 V, far less positive than +1.23 V for O₂/H₂O).
items.specStatementText: During electrolysis of aqueous solutions, competing reactions can occur at the anode and cathode, including the oxidation and reduction of water.
items.random_wrong: With copper electrodes, Cu²⁺ ions are reduced to copper at the anode.

items.q: When water is electrolysed, a little sulfuric acid is usually added. Hydrogen forms at the cathode and oxygen at the anode. What is the role of the sulfuric acid?
items.correct: It supplies ions so that the water conducts a useful current.
items.misconception: It is the source of the hydrogen and oxygen gases produced.
items.why: Students expect the 'active' substance added to be the one that reacts, and do not see that the ions can conduct without being discharged. The dissolved ions carry the current through the solution. At the electrodes, water is reduced to H₂ and oxidized to O₂, so the amount of acid stays the same.
items.specStatementText: During electrolysis of aqueous solutions, competing reactions can occur at the anode and cathode, including the oxidation and reduction of water.
items.random_wrong: It lets electrons travel through the water between the electrodes.

items.q: A steel key is electroplated with copper using a copper anode and CuSO₄(aq) as the electrolyte. Which half-equation shows the reaction at the key?
items.correct: Cu²⁺(aq) + 2e⁻ → Cu(s)
items.misconception: Cu(s) → Cu²⁺(aq) + 2e⁻
items.why: The four terms (anode, cathode, oxidation, reduction) are paired by rote and the pairs are easily swapped; there is no everyday meaning to anchor them. Anode and oxidation both begin with a vowel; reduction and cathode both begin with a consonant. The pairing holds in every electrochemical cell.
items.specStatementText: Electroplating involves the electrolytic coating of an object with a metallic thin layer.
items.random_wrong: Cu²⁺(aq) → Cu(s) + 2e⁻

items.q:
Na₂SO₄(aq) is electrolysed with inert electrodes.
Na⁺(aq) + e⁻ ⇌ Na(s)   E⦵ = −2.71 V
2H₂O(l) + 2e⁻ ⇌ H₂(g) + 2OH⁻(aq)   E⦵ = −0.83 V
O₂(g) + 4H⁺(aq) + 4e⁻ ⇌ 2H₂O(l)   E⦵ = +1.23 V
What forms at the cathode, and why?
items.correct: Hydrogen, as water is reduced more readily than Na⁺(aq) ions
items.misconception: Sodium, as the metal ion of the dissolved salt is reduced there
items.why: Electrolysis of molten salts, in which the metal is always formed at the cathode, is generalized to aqueous solutions, and movement of cations towards the cathode is taken to mean that they must react there. At the cathode the species most readily reduced reacts: compare the E⦵ of the metal ion with that of water. Ions of metals with very negative E⦵ values, such as Na⁺, are not reduced in aqueous solution; hydrogen forms instead.
items.specStatementText: During electrolysis of aqueous solutions, competing reactions can occur at the anode and cathode, including the oxidation and reduction of water.
items.random_wrong: Sodium, as Na⁺/Na has the E⦵ value that is largest in size

items.q: Which statement about primary cells and secondary (rechargeable) cells is correct?
items.correct: A primary cell costs less to buy but can never be reused once it runs down.
items.misconception: A secondary cell can be recharged endlessly with no loss of capacity.
items.why: The word 'rechargeable', and the idea that charging is the exact reverse of discharge, suggest that nothing is lost in each cycle. Charging reverses the main cell reaction, but not perfectly: side reactions and changes to the electrode surfaces build up, so the capacity falls and the cell eventually has to be replaced. This limited life is a disadvantage to weigh against reusability.
items.specStatementText: Secondary (rechargeable) cells involve redox reactions that can be reversed using electrical energy.
items.random_wrong: A primary cell holds a store of electricity that flows out until it is empty.

items.q: Nitrogen has the oxidation state −3 in ammonia, NH₃. What is the oxidation state of nitrogen in the nitrate ion, NO₃⁻?
items.why:
Main-group metals such as Na, Mg and Al do have a single oxidation state in their compounds, and for transition elements one familiar compound is often met far more than the others, so its value is memorized as 'the' oxidation state. Transition elements and most non-metals show variable oxidation states, which is why names carry Roman numerals. Deduce the state from the formula each time: in MnCl₂, x + 2(−1) = 0, so Mn is +2.

Working: Let the oxidation state of N be x. O is −2. Sum = charge on the ion: x + 3(−2) = −1, so x = +5.
items.specStatementText: Oxidation and reduction can be described in terms of electron transfer, change in oxidation state, oxygen gain/loss or hydrogen loss/gain.
items.working: Let the oxidation state of N be x. O is −2. Sum = charge on the ion: x + 3(−2) = −1, so x = +5.

items.q: A voltaic cell is to be built from a zinc electrode and a copper electrode, joined by a wire and by a salt bridge containing KNO₃(aq). Zinc is to be the anode. What should the half-cell containing the copper electrode consist of?
items.correct: Copper dipping into a solution containing Cu²⁺ ions
items.misconception: Copper dipping into a solution of zinc ions, Zn²⁺
items.why: Students look for a way for material to 'move' from one electrode to the other, and the salt bridge is the only visible connection between the solutions. The salt bridge contains an unreactive electrolyte. Its ions, not the zinc ions, move to keep the solutions neutral. Each metal ion is reduced only in its own half-cell.
items.specStatementText: A primary (voltaic) cell is an electrochemical cell that converts energy from spontaneous redox reactions to electrical energy.
items.random_wrong: Copper dipping into a beaker of distilled water

items.q: Propan-1-ol is heated with an acidified oxidizing agent in apparatus set up for distillation, and the distillate is collected. What is the main organic product collected, and why?
items.correct: Propanal, as it distils out before it can be oxidized further
items.misconception: Propanoic acid, as distillation keeps propanal in the flask
items.why: Both methods use a condenser and heating, and the difference (vertical condenser returning liquid versus a condenser leading to a collecting vessel) is remembered as a picture rather than by its purpose. Reflux = vapour returns to the flask, so the reaction goes to completion (carboxylic acid). Distillation = vapour is collected elsewhere, so the aldehyde escapes further oxidation.
items.specStatementText: Functional groups in organic compounds may undergo oxidation.
items.random_wrong: Propanone, as the alcohol is oxidized to a ketone

items.q: Oct-4-yne, CH₃CH₂CH₂C≡CCH₂CH₂CH₃, reacts completely with excess hydrogen in the presence of a nickel catalyst. What is the organic product?
items.correct: CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂CH₂CH₂CH₂CH₃
items.misconception: CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₃ and CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₃
items.why: A triple bond is drawn as three identical lines, so students assume all three are equivalent and all can react. The σ bond keeps the two carbon atoms joined. Hydrogenation converts C=C to C–C and C≡C to C–C, removing only the π bonds.
items.specStatementText: Reduction of unsaturated compounds by the addition of hydrogen lowers the degree of unsaturation.
items.random_wrong: CH₃CH₂CH₂CH=CHCH₂CH₂CH₃

items.q:
Standard electrode potentials:
Zn²⁺(aq) + 2e⁻ ⇌ Zn(s)   E⦵ = −0.76 V
Fe²⁺(aq) + 2e⁻ ⇌ Fe(s)   E⦵ = −0.45 V
Sn²⁺(aq) + 2e⁻ ⇌ Sn(s)   E⦵ = −0.14 V
Cu²⁺(aq) + 2e⁻ ⇌ Cu(s)   E⦵ = +0.34 V
Which reaction is spontaneous under standard conditions?
items.correct: Fe(s) + Sn²⁺(aq) → Fe²⁺(aq) + Sn(s)
items.misconception: Cu(s) + Sn²⁺(aq) → Cu²⁺(aq) + Sn(s)
items.why:
Combining two things suggests adding, and some textbooks reverse the sign of the anode potential and then add, which students half-remember as 'just add them'. Both tabulated values are reduction potentials. The anode reaction is an oxidation, so its value is subtracted: E⦵cell = E⦵(cathode) − E⦵(anode).

Working: E⦵cell = E⦵(cathode, species reduced) − E⦵(anode, species oxidized).
Fe + Zn²⁺ → Fe²⁺ + Zn: Zn²⁺ reduced, Fe oxidized: −0.76 − (−0.45) = −0.31 V (not spontaneous).
Fe + Sn²⁺ → Fe²⁺ + Sn: Sn²⁺ reduced, Fe oxidized: −0.14 − (−0.45) = +0.31 V (spontaneous).
Cu + Sn²⁺ → Cu²⁺ + Sn: Sn²⁺ reduced, Cu oxidized: −0.14 − (+0.34) = −0.48 V (not spontaneous).
Cu + Fe²⁺ → Cu²⁺ + Fe: Fe²⁺ reduced, Cu oxidized: −0.45 − (+0.34) = −0.79 V (not spontaneous).
Only Fe(s) + Sn²⁺(aq) has E⦵cell > 0.
items.specStatementText: Standard cell potential, E⦵cell, can be calculated from standard electrode potentials. E⦵cell has a positive value for a spontaneous reaction.
items.random_wrong: Fe(s) + Zn²⁺(aq) → Fe²⁺(aq) + Zn(s)
items.working:
E⦵cell = E⦵(cathode, species reduced) − E⦵(anode, species oxidized).
Fe + Zn²⁺ → Fe²⁺ + Zn: Zn²⁺ reduced, Fe oxidized: −0.76 − (−0.45) = −0.31 V (not spontaneous).
Fe + Sn²⁺ → Fe²⁺ + Sn: Sn²⁺ reduced, Fe oxidized: −0.14 − (−0.45) = +0.31 V (spontaneous).
Cu + Sn²⁺ → Cu²⁺ + Sn: Sn²⁺ reduced, Cu oxidized: −0.14 − (+0.34) = −0.48 V (not spontaneous).
Cu + Fe²⁺ → Cu²⁺ + Fe: Fe²⁺ reduced, Cu oxidized: −0.45 − (+0.34) = −0.79 V (not spontaneous).
Only Fe(s) + Sn²⁺(aq) has E⦵cell > 0.

items.q: For the reaction 2Al(s) + 3Sn²⁺(aq) → 2Al³⁺(aq) + 3Sn(s), ΔG⦵ = −880 kJ mol⁻¹. F = 96 500 C mol⁻¹. What is E⦵cell for this reaction?
items.why:
Half-equations are where students first see electrons written explicitly, and in the usual textbook examples (Zn/Cu²⁺, Mg/2H⁺) the electron count in each half-equation already equals n, so the need to scale the half-equations to the overall equation is never seen to matter. n is the number of moles of electrons transferred per mole of reaction as the overall equation is written. Scale the half-equations to a common number of electrons (×2 for Al, ×3 for Cu²⁺) and read n from that common number: 6. ΔG⦵ doubles if the equation is doubled; E⦵cell does not.

Working: Half-equations: 2Al → 2Al³⁺ + 6e⁻ and 3Sn²⁺ + 6e⁻ → 3Sn, so n = 6 mol of electrons per mole of reaction as written.
ΔG⦵ = −nFE⦵cell, so E⦵cell = −ΔG⦵/(nF).
ΔG⦵ = −880 kJ mol⁻¹ = −880 000 J mol⁻¹.
E⦵cell = 880 000 J mol⁻¹ / (6 × 96 500 C mol⁻¹) = 880 000 / 579 000 = 1.52 V (J C⁻¹ = V).
Consistency check: E⦵(Sn²⁺/Sn) − E⦵(Al³⁺/Al) = −0.14 − (−1.66) = +1.52 V.
items.specStatementText: The equation ΔG⦵ = −nFE⦵cell shows the relationship between standard change in Gibbs energy and standard cell potential for a reaction.
items.working:
Half-equations: 2Al → 2Al³⁺ + 6e⁻ and 3Sn²⁺ + 6e⁻ → 3Sn, so n = 6 mol of electrons per mole of reaction as written.
ΔG⦵ = −nFE⦵cell, so E⦵cell = −ΔG⦵/(nF).
ΔG⦵ = −880 kJ mol⁻¹ = −880 000 J mol⁻¹.
E⦵cell = 880 000 J mol⁻¹ / (6 × 96 500 C mol⁻¹) = 880 000 / 579 000 = 1.52 V (J C⁻¹ = V).
Consistency check: E⦵(Sn²⁺/Sn) − E⦵(Al³⁺/Al) = −0.14 − (−1.66) = +1.52 V.

items.q: A steel bracelet is to be electroplated with silver. It is placed in AgNO₃(aq) with a silver rod as the second electrode; the bracelet is connected to the negative terminal of a DC power supply and the silver rod to the positive terminal. Which statement about this cell is correct?
items.correct: The silver rod is the anode and dissolves, forming Ag⁺(aq) ions
items.misconception: The silver rod is the cathode, because Ag⁺(aq) ions are produced at it
items.why: The similar words are learned together ('cations go to the cathode') and the link is remembered as 'cations belong to the cathode' rather than as a statement about where they are reduced. Link electrode names only to the reaction: anode = oxidation (including metal atoms forming cations), cathode = reduction.
items.specStatementText: Electroplating involves the electrolytic coating of an object with a metallic thin layer.
items.random_wrong: The bracelet is the anode, because it is connected to the negative terminal

items.q: In working out oxidation states in an ion such as NH₄⁺ or MnO₄²⁻, what must the oxidation states add up to?
items.correct: The charge on the ion (+1 for NH₄⁺, −2 for MnO₄²⁻), not zero.
items.misconception: The oxidation states in any species add up to zero.
items.why: The first examples practised are neutral compounds (H₂O, CO₂, NaCl), for which the sum really is zero, and the rule is learned without its condition 'for a neutral species'. Oxidation states sum to zero only in a neutral compound or element. In an ion they sum to the charge on the ion: for NH₄⁺, x + 4(+1) = +1, so x = −3, not −4.
items.specStatementText: Oxidation and reduction can be described in terms of electron transfer, change in oxidation state, oxygen gain/loss or hydrogen loss/gain.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is the oxidation state of an atom the same as the number of bonds it forms?
items.correct: No. Nitrogen forms four bonds in NH₄⁺ but its oxidation state is −3; the oxidation state depends on which atoms are more electronegative, not on how many bonds there are.
items.misconception: The oxidation state of an atom equals the number of covalent bonds it forms (its valency).
items.why: The older term 'valency' was taught as the combining power of an element and is often given without a sign, so students treat 'number of bonds' and 'oxidation state' as the same idea. Oxidation state is found by assigning bonding electrons to the more electronegative atom. In NH₄⁺ each N–H bond's electrons are assigned to N, giving N −3, whatever the number of bonds.
items.specStatementText: Oxidation and reduction can be described in terms of electron transfer, change in oxidation state, oxygen gain/loss or hydrogen loss/gain.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: In Cl₂ + 2e⁻ → 2Cl⁻, which species is the oxidizing agent: Cl₂ or Cl⁻?
items.correct: Cl₂. The oxidizing agent is the reactant that accepts electrons; Cl⁻ is the product it forms.
items.misconception: The oxidizing agent is the species that ends up holding the gained electrons, i.e. the reduced product (Cl⁻ rather than Cl₂).
items.why: In the half-equation the electrons 'end up' on Cl⁻, so students look for the species carrying them rather than the reactant that accepted them. Agents are reactants. Identify which reactant is reduced (its oxidation state falls): that reactant is the oxidizing agent. Cl₂ (0) becomes Cl⁻ (−1), so Cl₂ is the oxidizing agent.
items.specStatementText: Oxidation and reduction can be described in terms of electron transfer, change in oxidation state, oxygen gain/loss or hydrogen loss/gain.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Can a reaction in which no oxygen is gained or lost be a redox reaction?
items.correct: Yes. Any reaction in which electrons are transferred, so oxidation states change, is redox, e.g. 2Fe²⁺ + Cl₂ → 2Fe³⁺ + 2Cl⁻.
items.misconception: Oxidation and reduction must involve gaining or losing oxygen, so a reaction without oxygen is not redox.
items.why: The everyday meaning of 'oxidation' (rusting, burning) and the first school definition (gain of oxygen) are both about oxygen, and the later electron-transfer definition is not integrated with them. The oxygen definition is a special case. The general definitions are electron transfer and change in oxidation state, which apply whether or not oxygen is present.
items.specStatementText: Oxidation and reduction can be described in terms of electron transfer, change in oxidation state, oxygen gain/loss or hydrogen loss/gain.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: In K₂Cr₂O₇, what is the oxidation state of chromium?
items.correct: +6. The two Cr atoms together contribute +12, so each Cr is +12/2 = +6.
items.misconception: The total contributed by all atoms of an element is its oxidation state (not divided by the number of atoms).
items.why: The sum rule is applied correctly but the last step, dividing by the subscript, is forgotten because in most practice examples there is only one atom of the element being found. An oxidation state is a value per atom. When there are n atoms of the element, divide their total contribution by n: Cr₂O₇²⁻ gives 2x − 14 = −2, x = +6.
items.specStatementText: Oxidation and reduction can be described in terms of electron transfer, change in oxidation state, oxygen gain/loss or hydrogen loss/gain.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: In a reduction half-equation, are electrons written as reactants or products?
items.correct: As reactants: reduction is gain of electrons, e.g. Cl₂ + 2e⁻ → 2Cl⁻.
items.misconception: Reduction is a loss (of electrons), so electrons appear as products in a reduction half-equation.
items.why: In everyday language 'reduce' means to make smaller or to lose something, and the oxygen definition of reduction (loss of oxygen) is also a loss, so reduction is remembered as 'losing'. Reduction is gain of electrons (the oxidation state is 'reduced' because negative electrons are added). Electrons are on the left of a reduction half-equation and on the right of an oxidation half-equation.
items.specStatementText: Half-equations separate the processes of oxidation and reduction, showing the loss or gain of electrons.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: When balancing charge in MnO₄⁻ + 8H⁺ + ne⁻ → Mn²⁺ + 4H₂O, is n the difference between the charges on MnO₄⁻ and Mn²⁺?
items.correct: No. The charge of the 8H⁺ must be included: left side −1 + 8 − n = +2 on the right, so n = 5.
items.misconception: Charge is balanced by comparing only the species containing the element that changes (MnO₄⁻ and Mn²⁺), ignoring the H⁺ ions added.
items.why: H⁺ and H₂O are added in the 'balance O and H' steps and are then treated as bookkeeping species that carry no charge in the final charge check. Balance charge using the TOTAL charge on each side, including every H⁺. Left: −1 + 8 = +7; right: +2; so 5e⁻ must be added to the left.
items.specStatementText: Half-equations separate the processes of oxidation and reduction, showing the loss or gain of electrons.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is a metal with more valence electrons oxidized more readily?
items.correct: No. Aluminium (three valence electrons) is oxidized less readily than sodium (one); more electrons to remove means more energy is needed.
items.misconception: A metal with more valence electrons has more electrons available to lose, so it is oxidized more readily.
items.why: Oxidation is described as losing electrons, so 'having more to lose' sounds like an advantage; the energy cost of removing each successive electron is not considered. Ease of oxidation depends on how strongly the outer electrons are held. Across a period nuclear charge increases and atoms shrink, so metals to the right (more valence electrons) hold their electrons more tightly.
items.specStatementText: The relative ease of oxidation and reduction of an element in a group can be predicted from its position in the periodic table. The reactions between metals and aqueous metal ions demonstrate the relative ease of oxidation of different metals.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is the metal seen reacting most dramatically in class (e.g. sodium in water) the most readily oxidized metal?
items.correct: Not necessarily. Metals lower in group 1 (rubidium, caesium) are oxidized even more readily than sodium but are too hazardous to demonstrate; ease of oxidation is predicted from position in the periodic table.
items.misconception: The metal whose reaction is most familiar or most dramatic in demonstrations (sodium in water, or iron visibly rusting) is the metal oxidized most readily.
items.why: Students judge reactivity from personal experience of reactions they have seen, and the most reactive metals are rarely shown, so the most vivid familiar example is taken as the extreme. Use periodic-table position: ease of oxidation increases down a group and towards the left of a period. Rubidium, below sodium in group 1, is oxidized more readily.
items.specStatementText: The relative ease of oxidation and reduction of an element in a group can be predicted from its position in the periodic table. The reactions between metals and aqueous metal ions demonstrate the relative ease of oxidation of different metals.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: When a halogen reacts as an oxidizing agent, which species is reduced: the halogen molecule or the halide ion?
items.correct: The halogen molecule (e.g. I₂ + 2e⁻ → 2I⁻). A halide ion already has a full outer shell and cannot be reduced further; it can only be oxidized.
items.misconception: Halide ions (Cl⁻, I⁻) are the species that are reduced, since they are the form that carries the negative charge.
items.why: The names 'iodine' and 'iodide' sound alike and are used loosely, and the negative charge on the halide is associated with reduction. Halogens (X₂, oxidation state 0) are reduced to halide ions (X⁻, −1). Halide ions are the reduced form; they can be oxidized back to the halogen but not reduced further.
items.specStatementText: The relative ease of oxidation and reduction of an element in a group can be predicted from its position in the periodic table. The reactions between metals and aqueous metal ions demonstrate the relative ease of oxidation of different metals.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Can a metal atom act as an oxidizing agent by accepting electrons?
items.correct: No. Metal atoms have no tendency to gain electrons to form negative ions in these reactions; they can only be oxidized (act as reducing agents). The oxidizing agents in displacement reactions are metal ions.
items.misconception: An unreactive metal holds electrons strongly, so the metal atom itself is a strong oxidizing agent that takes electrons from other metals.
items.why: 'Unreactive' is interpreted as 'holds on to electrons tightly', and holding electrons tightly is confused with pulling electrons from other species. An unreactive metal is one that is hard to oxidize. It is its ION that is a good oxidizing agent: Z²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Z proceeds readily when Z is unreactive.
items.specStatementText: The relative ease of oxidation and reduction of an element in a group can be predicted from its position in the periodic table. The reactions between metals and aqueous metal ions demonstrate the relative ease of oxidation of different metals.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is the hydrogen released by a metal and acid given off as H atoms?
items.correct: No. Hydrogen is released as diatomic H₂ molecules: 2H⁺(aq) + 2e⁻ → H₂(g). Likewise iodide is oxidized to I₂, not I.
items.misconception: Non-metal elements formed in a reaction are written as single atoms (H, I), one for each ion discharged.
items.why: Each H⁺ (or I⁻) gains (or loses) one electron, so the product is written as a single atom; the fact that these elements are diatomic is not applied when writing the equation. Hydrogen, nitrogen, oxygen and the halogens exist as diatomic molecules. Two H⁺ ions gain two electrons to form one H₂ molecule; two I⁻ ions lose two electrons to form one I₂ molecule.
items.specStatementText: Acids react with reactive metals to release hydrogen.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What are the products when a reactive metal reacts with a dilute acid?
items.correct: A salt and hydrogen gas, e.g. Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂.
items.misconception: Metal + acid gives a salt and water, as in a neutralization.
items.why: Students learn several acid reactions together (acid + base → salt + water; acid + carbonate → salt + water + carbon dioxide) and the 'salt + water' pattern is over-applied to metals. A metal contains no oxygen or hydroxide, so no water can form. The metal is oxidized and the H⁺ ions are reduced to hydrogen gas: M + 2H⁺ → M²⁺ + H₂.
items.specStatementText: Acids react with reactive metals to release hydrogen.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is oxidation the gain or the loss of electrons?
items.correct: Loss. Oxidation is loss of electrons (and reduction is gain).
items.misconception: Oxidation is gain of electrons, by analogy with oxidation as gain of oxygen.
items.why: The oxygen definition (gain of oxygen) is learned first, and 'gain' is carried over to electrons, reversing the electron definition. Oxidation is loss of electrons: the oxidation state rises because negative charge is removed. Example: 2Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 2e⁻.
items.specStatementText: Oxidation occurs at the anode and reduction occurs at the cathode in electrochemical cells.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Do anions in the salt bridge of a voltaic cell move towards the positive electrode (cathode)?
items.correct: No. Anions move towards the ANODE half-cell, where cations are being produced and positive charge is building up in solution.
items.misconception: Ions in the salt bridge move towards the electrode of opposite charge, so anions move to the positive cathode.
items.why: In electrolysis ions are described as being attracted to oppositely charged electrodes, and this picture is transferred to the salt bridge of a voltaic cell. Ion movement in the salt bridge is driven by charge build-up in the solutions: the anode solution gains cations (Zn²⁺), so anions move there; the cathode solution loses cations (Cu²⁺), so cations move there.
items.specStatementText: A primary (voltaic) cell is an electrochemical cell that converts energy from spontaneous redox reactions to electrical energy.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: To reverse a half-equation, is it enough to move the electrons to the other side?
items.correct: No. The whole equation is reversed: all reactants become products, including the electrons.
items.misconception: A half-equation is reversed by moving only the electrons to the other side, leaving the other species where they are.
items.why: Students remember that 'reversing changes where the electrons are' and apply this as the whole rule. Reversing means swapping the entire left and right sides. Pb + SO₄²⁻ → PbSO₄ + 2e⁻ reversed is PbSO₄ + 2e⁻ → Pb + SO₄²⁻.
items.specStatementText: Secondary (rechargeable) cells involve redox reactions that can be reversed using electrical energy.

items.q: Is a hydrogen fuel cell free of all environmental impact because its only product is water?
items.correct: No. The cell's product is water, but producing, compressing and transporting the hydrogen uses energy, and most hydrogen is currently made from fossil fuels.
items.misconception: Because the only product of a hydrogen fuel cell is water, using it causes no pollution at all.
items.why: Hydrogen is presented in the media as a 'clean' fuel, and attention is focused on the reaction in the cell rather than on the whole supply chain. Judge a cell on its whole life cycle. The disadvantages of hydrogen fuel cells include the energy and emissions involved in producing and storing hydrogen.

items.q: Does a hydrogen fuel cell burn hydrogen?
items.correct: No. Hydrogen is oxidized at the anode and oxygen reduced at the cathode in separate half-cells, so chemical energy is converted directly into electrical energy without combustion.
items.misconception: A fuel cell burns its fuel and converts the heat released into electricity, like a power station.
items.why: The word 'fuel' is associated with burning, and the overall equation 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O is the same as for combustion. In a fuel cell the two half-reactions happen at different electrodes and the electrons pass through the external circuit. There is no flame, and there is no heat-to-electricity conversion step.

items.q: Does the electric current create the ions in an electrolyte?
items.correct: No. The ions are already present in the molten or dissolved ionic compound; the current makes them move and brings about their discharge at the electrodes.
items.misconception: Passing a current splits the compound into ions, and these ions then carry the current.
items.why: The word 'electrolysis' (splitting by electricity) suggests that the current does the splitting, including the splitting into ions. Ionic compounds consist of ions in the solid. Melting or dissolving frees them to move. The current then drives the ions to the electrodes, where they are oxidized or reduced.
items.specStatementText: An electrolytic cell is an electrochemical cell that converts electrical energy to chemical energy by bringing about non-spontaneous reactions.

items.q: In the electrolysis of an aqueous solution, is water always the species oxidized and reduced?
items.correct: No. Water competes with the ions of the solute and does not always react: Cl⁻ is oxidized in concentrated NaCl(aq), and Cu²⁺ is reduced in CuSO₄(aq).
items.misconception: Electrolysis always produces hydrogen and oxygen from water, whatever the electrolyte.
items.why: The electrolysis of water is often the first electrolysis demonstration seen, and hydrogen and oxygen become the expected products of any electrolysis. Identify every species present. In an aqueous solution water is only one of the species that can react at each electrode; compare E⦵ values (and, for NaCl(aq), the concentration) to decide which one reacts.
items.specStatementText: During electrolysis of aqueous solutions, competing reactions can occur at the anode and cathode, including the oxidation and reduction of water.

items.q: Is the oxidation of an alcohol a reaction with oxygen gas, as in combustion?
items.correct: No. Under laboratory conditions the alcohol is oxidized by an oxidizing agent in solution, forming an aldehyde, ketone or carboxylic acid; combustion in O₂ is a different reaction giving CO₂ and H₂O.
items.misconception: Oxidation of an organic compound means reaction with oxygen gas, from the air, giving carbon dioxide and water as in combustion.
items.why: Combustion is the first organic 'oxidation' students meet, and the word oxidation suggests that oxygen gas must be involved. In organic chemistry, oxidation is gain of oxygen or loss of hydrogen by the functional group. [O] represents oxygen supplied by an oxidizing agent, and the carbon skeleton is kept.

items.q: Can every alcohol be oxidized to a carboxylic acid if it is heated for long enough?
items.correct: No. Only primary alcohols give carboxylic acids; secondary alcohols stop at ketones and tertiary alcohols are not oxidized under similar conditions.
items.misconception: Any alcohol is oxidized all the way to a carboxylic acid if heated under reflux for long enough.
items.why: Ethanol, the alcohol used in most examples, does go to ethanoic acid on reflux, and the rate of reaction is confused with whether the reaction is possible at all. Each oxidation step removes a hydrogen atom from the carbon bearing the OH (or adds O there). A tertiary carbon has no such hydrogen, and a ketone carbon cannot gain another O without breaking a C–C bond.

items.q: Is the aldehyde always the final product of oxidizing a primary alcohol?
items.correct: No. The aldehyde is the final product only if it is distilled off as it forms; under reflux it is oxidized further to the carboxylic acid.
items.misconception: Oxidizing a primary alcohol always stops at the aldehyde.
items.why: The first step (alcohol → aldehyde) is usually taught first and in most detail, and the second step is treated as an optional extra. The product depends on conditions. Distillation gives the aldehyde; reflux with excess oxidizing agent gives the carboxylic acid.

items.q: Does reduction of a carbonyl compound add oxygen to it?
items.correct: No. Reduction adds hydrogen (or removes oxygen); adding oxygen is oxidation.
items.misconception: Reduction of a carbonyl compound adds oxygen, converting it to a carboxylic acid.
items.why: The terms oxidation and reduction are both new in organic contexts and are easily swapped, particularly when the oxygen and hydrogen definitions are remembered only vaguely. Reduction = gain of hydrogen or loss of oxygen. Butanone + 2[H] → butan-2-ol is reduction; forming an acid would require oxidation.

items.q: Is a hydride ion, H⁻, the same as a proton, H⁺?
items.correct: No. H⁻ has two electrons and is negatively charged; H⁺ is a bare proton. Hydride ions add hydrogen with its electron pair to the C=O carbon.
items.misconception: A hydride ion is a hydrogen ion that behaves like an acid, donating H⁺.
items.why: Both are called 'hydrogen ions' informally, and students have met H⁺ far more often, so any ionic hydrogen is assumed to be a proton. Check the charge: H⁻ carries an extra electron and is a source of electron-rich hydrogen, so it reduces the compound; H⁺ is an acid.

items.q: Is a reagent written above the reaction arrow a catalyst?
items.correct: Not necessarily. Reagents such as the hydride source are written above the arrow for convenience but are consumed in the reaction.
items.misconception: Anything written above the arrow in an equation is a catalyst that is not used up.
items.why: Catalysts (e.g. Ni in hydrogenation) are written above the arrow, and the same position is used for reagents and conditions, so the two are confused. Ask whether the substance is regenerated. The hydride source is used up (it is the reducing agent); a catalyst such as nickel is not.

items.q: Does reduction remove all the oxygen from a ketone or a carboxylic acid, forming an alkane?
items.correct: No. A ketone is reduced to a secondary alcohol, and a carboxylic acid via the aldehyde to a primary alcohol; both products still contain oxygen.
items.misconception: Reduction removes all the oxygen from a compound, so a carbonyl compound or carboxylic acid is reduced to an alkane.
items.why: 'Reduction is loss of oxygen' is taken to mean loss of ALL the oxygen, and the alcohol is not seen as the end point. Reduction of a C=O group adds hydrogen across it, and the oxygen stays as an OH group: a ketone gives a secondary alcohol, and a carboxylic acid is reduced via the aldehyde to a primary alcohol.

items.q: Can the absolute potential of a single half-cell be measured?
items.correct: No. Only a potential difference between two electrodes can be measured, so a reference half-cell is needed and assigned 0 V.
items.misconception: Each half-cell has a potential that can be measured on its own, and the hydrogen half-cell happens to measure zero.
items.why: Tables of E⦵ values look like measured properties of each half-cell, like melting points, so students assume each is measured individually. A voltmeter needs two connections, so it measures a difference. E⦵ values are differences from the standard hydrogen electrode, which is 0 V by definition.
items.specStatementText: The hydrogen half-cell H⁺(aq) + e⁻ ⇌ ½H₂(g) is assigned a standard electrode potential of zero by convention. It is used in the measurement of standard electrode potential, E⦵.

items.q: Is the E⦵ of the hydrogen electrode zero because platinum is inert?
items.correct: No. Platinum is used because it is inert and conducts, but the 0 V is a convention for the H⁺/H₂ couple, not a consequence of platinum's inertness.
items.misconception: The standard hydrogen electrode has zero potential because the platinum electrode does not react.
items.why: The inert platinum electrode is the most visible part of the apparatus, and 'does not react' is linked to 'gives no potential'. Platinum only provides a surface for H⁺/H₂ electron exchange. Other half-cells with platinum (e.g. Fe³⁺/Fe²⁺) have non-zero E⦵, showing the platinum does not set the value.
items.specStatementText: The hydrogen half-cell H⁺(aq) + e⁻ ⇌ ½H₂(g) is assigned a standard electrode potential of zero by convention. It is used in the measurement of standard electrode potential, E⦵.

items.q: In the couple Ag⁺ + e⁻ ⇌ Ag (E⦵ = +0.80 V), is Ag(s) the oxidizing agent indicated by the positive E⦵?
items.correct: No. E⦵ refers to the reduction of the species on the LEFT. A positive value means Ag⁺ is readily reduced, so Ag⁺ is the oxidizing agent; Ag(s) is a weak reducing agent.
items.misconception: The E⦵ value describes the element (the right-hand species) of the couple, so the metal with the most positive E⦵ is the strongest oxidizing agent.
items.why: Couples are often labelled by the element name ('the silver electrode'), so the value is attached to the metal rather than to the ion on the left of the half-equation. Write the half-equation: oxidized form + e⁻ ⇌ reduced form. The oxidizing agent is always the species on the left; the more positive E⦵, the stronger it is.

items.q: Is E⦵cell calculated as E⦵(anode) − E⦵(cathode)?
items.correct: No. E⦵cell = E⦵(cathode) − E⦵(anode), where the cathode is where reduction occurs.
items.misconception: E⦵cell is calculated as E⦵(anode) − E⦵(cathode), i.e. the two electrode roles are swapped in the subtraction.
items.why: The order of subtraction is remembered without its meaning, and cathode and anode are easily swapped. Identify the species reduced (cathode) and oxidized (anode) in the reaction as written. E⦵cell = E⦵(reduction) − E⦵(oxidation). A positive result means the reaction is spontaneous as written.
items.specStatementText: Standard cell potential, E⦵cell, can be calculated from standard electrode potentials. E⦵cell has a positive value for a spontaneous reaction.

items.q: Is a reaction spontaneous when E⦵cell is negative, as it is when ΔG⦵ is negative?
items.correct: No. A reaction is spontaneous when E⦵cell is POSITIVE. Because ΔG⦵ = −nFE⦵cell, a positive E⦵cell corresponds to a negative ΔG⦵.
items.misconception: A negative E⦵cell means the reaction is spontaneous (and a positive value means the reverse is spontaneous), just as for ΔG⦵.
items.why: Students learn 'negative ΔG⦵ means spontaneous' in energetics and transfer the sign rule to E⦵cell without noticing the minus sign in ΔG⦵ = −nFE⦵cell. The two quantities have opposite signs for the same reaction. Spontaneous: E⦵cell > 0 and ΔG⦵ < 0.

items.q: Are anions of the solute always oxidized at the anode in aqueous electrolysis?
items.correct: No. Sulfate ions are not oxidized in aqueous solution; water is oxidized in preference (to O₂) at an inert anode.
items.misconception: The anion of the dissolved salt is always the species discharged at the anode, because anions are attracted there.
items.why: Movement of anions towards the anode is taken to mean that they must react there. Movement and reaction are different. At the anode, the species most easily oxidized reacts: for SO₄²⁻ solutions, that is water (or a reactive anode material).
items.specStatementText: During electrolysis of aqueous solutions, competing reactions can occur at the anode and cathode, including the oxidation and reduction of water.

items.q: How is the mole ratio from a balanced equation used to find the amount of a product?
items.correct: n(product) = n(reactant) × coefficient of product ÷ coefficient of reactant. For 2Al + 3H₂SO₄ → Al₂(SO₄)₃ + 3H₂, n(H₂) = n(Al) × 3/2.
items.misconception: The mole ratio is applied upside down: amount of product = amount of reactant × (coefficient of reactant ÷ coefficient of product).
items.why: Students remember that a ratio of coefficients is used but not which way up; inverting or ignoring the mole ratio is a widely reported procedural error in stoichiometry. Write the ratio with the unknown on top: n(H₂) ÷ n(Al) = 3 ÷ 2, so n(H₂) = n(Al) × 3/2. Check: the equation shows more H₂ than Al, so the amount of H₂ must be larger than the amount of Al.

items.q: Which alcohols are oxidized by an acidified oxidizing agent?
items.correct: Primary and secondary alcohols are oxidized; tertiary alcohols are not oxidized under similar conditions, because the C–OH carbon has no H atom.
items.misconception: Only primary alcohols are oxidized by acidified oxidizing agents; secondary and tertiary alcohols are not.
items.why: Ethanol, a primary alcohol, is the standard example (breathalyser, vinegar), and the fact that tertiary alcohols resist oxidation is over-extended to every non-primary alcohol. Oxidation removes a hydrogen atom from the carbon bearing the OH group. Primary and secondary alcohols have at least one H on that carbon, so both are oxidized (to an aldehyde and a ketone respectively); a tertiary alcohol has none.

items.q: What is the organic product when but-2-yne, CH₃C≡CCH₃, reacts completely with excess hydrogen over a nickel catalyst?
items.correct: Butane, CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₃. Hydrogenation adds H₂ across the multiple bond only: two H₂ molecules convert the triple bond into a single bond. No oxygen is added, so no alcohol can form.
items.misconception: Hydrogenation is the same reaction as hydration: reacting an alkene or alkyne with hydrogen adds H and OH across the multiple bond, giving an alcohol.
items.why: The names hydrogenation, hydration and hydrolysis look and sound alike and are all met as reactions of the same functional groups, so students merge them into one 'add hydro-something' reaction; the everyday link between 'hydro-' and water pushes the merged reaction towards adding water. Hydrogenation adds H₂ (two H atoms) across a C=C or C≡C bond and lowers the degree of unsaturation, giving an alkene or alkane. Hydration adds H₂O (H and OH) to an alkene, giving an alcohol. Hydrogen gas contains no oxygen, so hydrogenation can never produce an OH group.

items.q: In 2Al(s) + 3Cu²⁺(aq) → 2Al³⁺(aq) + 3Cu(s), the half-equations show 3e⁻ (Al → Al³⁺ + 3e⁻) and 2e⁻ (Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu). Is n = 3 + 2 = 5?
items.correct: No, n = 6. The electrons lost by aluminium are the same electrons gained by copper ions, so they are counted once. Scaling the half-equations to a common 6e⁻ gives n = 6.
items.misconception: n is the total of the electrons shown in the two half-equations added together (3 + 2 = 5), because electrons are 'involved' at both electrodes.
items.why: Electrons appear on the product side of one half-equation and the reactant side of the other, so students treat them as two separate sets and add them, as they would add up reactants; that the electrons lost at the anode are the very electrons gained at the cathode is rarely made explicit. One set of electrons is transferred from the reducing agent to the oxidizing agent. Balance the half-equations so that the electrons cancel (6e⁻ lost, 6e⁻ gained) and n is that common number, 6, not the sum of the two.
